utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit. And you may begin, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Good afternoon. I wish to tell you one matter. Since the other witness had protective measures, can you please accept his position, which at present is that the protective measures be lifted and that he testify without any protective measures, and I'm referring to the next witness in line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's for the next witness, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness T-25. Can you please state your full name to the Judges?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: My name is Milorad Kosarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I asked you this morning that you wait for the transcript to stop before answering. You were born on the 12th of July, 1950; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Once again, please wait with your answer before the cursor stops. You were born in the municipality of Ilijas in Sarajevo; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do not hurry with your answer because as we broach the relevant topics we won't be able to proceed at a normal pace. Therefore, I repeat: Do not give your answer before you see the cursor stop. Wait for a second or two before giving your answer. You completed your primary school in Vogosca, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You completed the school for teachers in Sarajevo, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see the cursor stop after you gave your answer, so please bear that in mind. At the time of the outbreak of the conflict you were the head master or principal of nursery or pre-school education in Vogosca, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, you lived in downtown Vogosca in a flat, while your family home was being built at the time and it was also located in Vogosca, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you now answer this first question of mine. Have you ever been working for the police as a person with an educational background as a teacher?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you join the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps in any capacity and, if so, when?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: I joined the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps in 1992 in May.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us why?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: I could not believe that there would be a war on. However, clashes broke out, people were killed, the situation was such that a person could not distance oneself from what was going on. There had been persons killed at the very start, civilians who were killed in their places of residence. Some of my relatives were even killed. I simply could not bear that situation any longer and I joined my people in a war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let us go through this quickly. Can you give us a couple of examples dating from those early days and in relation to the matters you've just raised?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm rising because I'm wondering why and what bearing it has to the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, can you answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can. For a long time this has not been a problem before this Trial Chamber. I believe it very important to know why an individual decides to take up arms. Let me repeat once more. This is the end of trial. I would not be dealing with all these matters had not the amended indictment from late 1996 state the matters as it does, and--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, this is marginally relevant. Just move through it quickly. And if the witness has evidence dealing with the later dates, 1994 and 1995, let us get to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked the witness to go through this as quickly as possible. But let me go to the heart of the matter, because there are some things I cannot deal with unless we go through these matters beforehand.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So please answer my question as briefly as possible, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: I had to join the war because I had no other choice. Fighting had already started, people were getting killed or wounded, and one could not stay aside, keep out of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let us not dwell on this. Which brigade were you a member of at the beginning of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: The Vogosca Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What were you doing for a while within the Vogosca Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: For a while, I performed the duties of an assistant for moral guidance and political affairs, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And for how long?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: For about a month.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And why so short?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: There was such dirty business going on in the area such as the theft of vehicles, and I simply could not deal with these matters. I asked that I do what I can do, that I go to the trenches.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And so where did you go to after a month had elapsed?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: I was in an area within the Vogosca municipality to the right of the traffic faculty, to the left, towards Zuc and to the right --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness please repeat the name of the last locality.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Repeat the name of the last place that you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The last place I mentioned is Hotonj.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I will be asking you to explain that more closely. However, I asked you what you were doing, what position you held, and I didn't mean the location. I meant what your role was through to the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: I was a fighter in a trench.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know when Dragomir Milosevic became the commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: In early August 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What was the brigade called at the time and what did it consist of?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: It was the 3rd Sarajevo Brigade, into which three brigades had been fused, Rajlovac -- the Rajlovac Brigade, Vogosca Brigade and the Kosevo Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you now explain to the Judges where the trenches were located, the ones in which you spent the entire war?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: This is an area from Vogosca to the right-hand side all the way to Zuc hill, the area beneath is called Perivoj, all the way to the left flank to the place called Hotonj which is to the east of Vogosca. And the neighbourhood in front of Vogosca is called Fabrika factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges when the lines where your trenches were in which you spent the rest of the war were in fact consolidated?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: The lines were definitely consolidated sometime in 1995. Up until that point there had been constant fighting and going to and fro in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please, you said in late 1995. My question was when were the lines formed before you went into the trenches there? When were they formed in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: At the very start of the war, the lines were set up and they moved to and fro but in a negligible way. There was every day fighting going on along the lines. It was only in 1995 that the situation became more stable.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In 1995 the war ended..

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: Until an attack was launched from all directions, from all sides upon that area, that's what I had in mind when I said 1995. I didn't mean the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know if you understand me correctly. I am asking you about 1992, and when was it that the separation lines were consolidated in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: As soon as the war started, the lines were set up there, and they changed slightly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And what happened in December of 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: In December of 1995, the positions on the right flank were captured by the BH army, thus moving the positions of the VRS significantly behind what was initially the line from the elevation point 850 to Gola Brda, Gola hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And when were the positions then consolidated?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: In the month of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And what was going on throughout 1992 until the month of December, and I mean what happened to the positions?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours. If we could just sort of pinpoint maybe some points in time. I understood we were talking about December 1995, which would put the testimony after the end of the conflict in the former Yugoslavia, and we're going back to 1992 but then talking about something that -- positions from 1992 all the way through to 1995, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Or is it to December 1992? Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely. I believe it is just a slip, a slip of the tongue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can I ask you once again when was at the start of the conflict in 1992 that the lines were set up which then did not change until the end of the conflict? First you said 1995 and then you spoke about 1992. The war ended in 1995. Can you be more specific in that regard?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: I don't think that I really understand you properly. I explained, the lines moved. The lines where I was were set up immediately when the conflict started and from that moment on until 1995, when they consolidated finally, they did not change. There had been movements, maybe 500 metres here or there, maybe a hill would be captured or not, but the lines did not move significantly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I have to ask just one more question. I wasted so much time on this. In this trench where you were, when did you definitely find yourself in in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: In May, late May.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell me what did those positions look like, the trenches? What did it look like? How far was it from the positions in relation to the positions that you mentioned Zuc, Hum? What did it look like on the spot while you were in the trenches?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The witness never once mentioned the name Hum during the course of his testimony so far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: He mentioned Zuc.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But not Hum.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My mistake. I should ask him about Zuc.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Then Zuc.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: We had those trenches that had been dug and we were able to establish visual contact and we could hear the other side. On some stretches the distance between the two -- the two lines was 50 or 100 metres but in many places we were in immediate vicinity.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So you were able to even communicate. Could you please give me an example. What did it look like at one point in the period while Dragomir Milosevic was the commander?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: I was in a trench near the cargo gate of the TAS factory, and it was during the cease-fire, and at around 9.00 a.m., a group of soldiers came by and I waved at them and I said, Hey, and one of them waved back and he responded. It was cease-fire, cease-fire was on and there was no shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please. But who -- whose soldiers? Who did the soldiers belong to? You said just a group of soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: It was a group of soldier of the BH army and they were in the immediate vicinity in a small alley-way leading from the traffic faculty to the right to Manjak [phoen] and we were able to see each other quite clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did anything happen there when you had this encounter with them?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: Not at that time. But at around 12.30, when our food came in, a sniper fired a shot at me, and he hit the man who was with me in the trench, a man by the name of Jozo Ivanic, an ethnic Croat. He hit me, despite the fact that we had communicated earlier. And I would like to note that they were so visible, so exposed that had we fired on them, we would have wiped them out because they were on the road. They had no cover, but we didn't do anything. But then, at half past 12.00, a sniper fired his shot at my back. I was in the trench. I was about to receive my meal, and Joso came out of the trench to get his food and his ration and then he was shot by this sniper.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But why are you telling us this? What was in force at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: I said that the cease-fire was in force, and there was no fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And in those days, could you please tell us what -- when did this incident occur?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: It was in 1994, in the summer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. And in those days or on that day, did anyone come to see you from the command?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: The accused was touring the Republika Srpska army positions and he came to the command where there was a notice board with lists. People would get their medical certificates there, their travel orders and so on, and there was a copy of the excerpt from the Geneva Conventions on the rules of waging the war. And when the accused came in, the notice board was behind the door, and he asked why is it there? Why hasn't it posted in a more visible place to the left where it would be more visible? Why does -- somebody should be looking at it and I now have to apologise, because when he left people said, Well is this guy normal or what? These other guys are violating the cease-fire. One of our guys was just shot, and this commander is asking the battalion where I was to -- to do this, to comply with all this. So this was the comment made by the people who were in the command at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This was the comment when he left?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And did he come there on any other occasions in your presence, and, in particular, while you were manning the positions?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: Yes. I saw the accused several times. At least five or six times I saw the accused when he toured the lines, particularly that area where I was, and I remember that we tried to improve our positions. We had this earth moving equipment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, not in the 65 ter summary -- and I'm reluctant to go down this road again, Your Honours, bit this is extreme because there was not one single mention in the 65 ter summary for this witness about any contact with the accused. In fact, we had received additional information about this man's function during the course of the war, because I had made a request for additional information earlier on this morning, and in that information there was no mention whatsoever of any contact with the accused at any time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I completed my proofing session with the witness a little while before 1.00 p.m. That was my first interview with this witness, because at the time when we got his details we didn't have an opportunity to do so. I talked to him for several hours this morning, and I completed this interview just before coming here, and now I don't know, was I supposed to write down everything that I would be examining this witness about, including about the events in the trench when the visit from the commanding officers occurred. It would have taken me one day just to inform the Prosecutor about all the things that I intend to examine this witness on. This has really gone beyond any bounds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I don't consider that you're severely prejudiced by this information, even if you are not informed about the contact of this witness with the accused. I believe you should be in a position to cross-examine on it. You have very good resources. I see two to my right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, how many times did you meet the commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, and what was discussed when he would come to the trenches?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: I would encounter the accused on the lines and before the war I didn't know him. But this is really characteristic, because in order to improve the position, there were some -- there was some rubber tires put on this earth-moving equipment. Some metal sheath and some sandbags and then this man said, Well, this is really stupid on your part. The engine will be overburdened and it would just break down. Had anyone -- if this had been possible to do, they would have done that earlier. The engineers would have come up with that. It often happened at the trenches --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, witness, please speak a little slower. Speak more slowly. The interpreter is having difficulty keeping up with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, was he ever in a trench during the fighting?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: Yes, during the fighting, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I was going to ask for a reformulation of the question because, as phrased, it calls for speculation, Your Honours, in my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, how do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, because I saw him. I was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Move on. And I should say, I'm going to apply the time-limits very strictly. You have one hour and 15 minutes each. We're going to take the first break at 3.20.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will be finished earlier than that, Your Honour, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What would he tell you during the fighting, as you explained to us? What would he tell you while he was there in the trenches?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: Unlike many others, I remember quite clearly, and I can state with absolute certainty that his suggestions would always be, first of all, to take care. He would always say that the cover should be improved and that nobody should be responsible enough to get out in the open. When we asked him when this all would end, because we have had -- we had had our fill of everything, he'd say that the politicians would have to solve this and that this would have to end soon. And of course he had to field some unpleasant questions, such as, for instance, that we have bad quality boots, that the food is not good, and that there are deserters, profiteers. He had to deal with issues of that sort but he would always be say, Be patient, take care, and we should try and stay alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And could you -- do you recall his response? Did you personally hear his response when he learned about a bad incident, an unpleasant incident, that occurred in Vogosca during his tenure as the commander? If you remember that, could you please tell the Judges?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: A crime was committed in Vogosca against Himza Ljubovic and his wife, two civilians. His wife's name was Fatima. They were honest people. Himza was the school principal and Fatima was a shopkeeper. These people were really good people. When we learned about this incident all those who lived in Vogosca and who knew the family had to be shocked, outraged and we, the fighters, demanded that the perpetrator be identified as soon as possible. I remember during the tour that we made this demand and he said, Oh my God, who did that? And why hasn't this been solved already? Is it impossible to identify the perpetrator? This should have been done already. And I have to say that to the end of my life, I will insist on it, and I am ready to testify in this case to make sure that whoever did this receives proper punishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But can you tell me, during the period while Dragomir Milosevic was the commander, this terrible crime happened, this is undoubtedly an outrageous crime. During the time while Dragomir Milosevic was responsible, were there any such incidents in the area of responsibility of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps with the exception of these two horrible murders?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In fact, Your Honours, I would suggest that's a leading question because nowhere in the testimony has the witness said that there were murders at issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, you -- maybe it's end of session blues. And I haven't heard the witness say that there was a murder. Did you? No. We heard testimony of a crime, a horrible crime being committed, somewhat so that my colleague to my left asking what happened, asking me informally what happened. Well, what happened, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Himza Ljubovic and his wife Fatima were killed, murdered. They were civilians who lived in Vogosca during the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Since I heard this in my native tongue, I understood that murders were involved. He said that there was a terrible crime, that everybody was outraged. Whether he also used the term murder or not, I'm not sure. But let me ask you, now, were there other such incidents in the area of responsibility of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps at any point in time during Dragomir Milosevic's tenure there?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: I know about this particular case for sure, whereas I do not wish to testify or speculate about matters I'm not certain of.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us something about the fighting that would take place in -- at the positions where you were. What were they like, these clashes?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: At the beginning of the war --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, perhaps for all of us the witness could, in his answer be asked to specify exactly where he is talking about when he talks about the positions he was at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. But maybe you're anticipating too much.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, yes. Mr. Tapuskovic will, no doubt, be dealing with that. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, sir, the trenches where you were at, were you there all the time or did you go elsewhere, to some other positions, other trenches?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: In my evidence, I stated the perimeter of the trenches where I was. I could have been in this one over there or in this once over there but always in that area, in that general area of the battlefield. I could have been in any of the trenches in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what sort of weapons were there in the area of responsibility of your brigade? And let me not make this a leading question, but at the time when the conflict broke out, up until a certain point in time, perhaps you should yourself specify the time, if you can. But can you tell us what it looked like at the outset?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: At the start we had infantry weapons, whatever infantry sorties would have. We had mortars. There was heavy weaponry there, such as tanks and Howitzers. We had these weapons until the pullout of heavy weaponry was stipulated and signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You told us that General Dragomir Milosevic took up his duties in August. What was the situation at that point in time? What sort of weapons did you have at your positions?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: I know that the mass media reported that there was an exclusion zone of 20 kilometres and there was no heavy weaponry there at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any sort of support in combat in the early days? And I'm referring to the period of time as you yourself specified it into different segments.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: If you're referring to artillery support, then, yes, we had that sort of support.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When Dragomir Milosevic took up his commanding duties, did you have that sort of support as well?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: We were not able to have that sort of support since the weapons had been taken away.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what happened in 1995 at some point, or can you tell us what the year 1995 was like at the very start?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: At the beginning of 1995, there was a cease-fire. I remember the year 1995 by the offensive. At the time I was at the positions near Golo Brdo, and I was a participant in that offensive. I was defending myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And did you have any artillery support in that offensive?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: Yes, we did, but I don't know --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: We have to use up our time efficiently. Prosecutor will have to ask their questions. You told us that there was this part of the year of 1995 when there was a cease-fire on. Do you recall the events related to a feature in the centre of Vogosca at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: I lived right next to the sports hall in Vogosca. That sports hall or gym was shelled as was the football stadium. The building where I lived was between these two buildings. Some individuals were wounded and extensive damage was inflicted on the buildings. My wife survived the attack by pure chance, because our balcony was hit and there was a bar which almost hit her. There was a boy who was wounded and my son had been grazed by a piece of shrapnel. It was all by pure chance that he was somewhere.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear where.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So he wasn't killed. There was other shelling of Vogosca, random and discriminate -- deliberate and indiscriminate. There was a person by the name of Djuric that was killed. There was a Vito from the post office who was also killed and this was all the result of indiscriminate shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And this was in time of a -- rather, this was while a cease-fire was on?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: Yes, during cease-fire too.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned an offensive. Can you tell us who mounted the offensive, which side? And I'm referring to the offensive that occurred in the summer of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: This was an offensive against all the positions of VRS from the positions where I was, all the way the entire length of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Who mounted the offensive? That's what you were asked. Who started the offensive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The forces of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I have to ask you something else before I forget. You mentioned the events concerning the gym, the sports hall. Was there something else that involved UNPROFOR in that same time-period?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: I was a sportsman in Vogosca. I was involved in sports activities and this was in addition to other charity work I did. I led a football club. Dela Prela, he was a captain, I don't recall his first name. The -- he was the commander of the French battalion that was there at Vogosca and he invited us to organise a football match and we provided the French battalion with the necessary equipment and we played a match. He was the one who interceded in order to make sure that there was no fighting during the football match. However during the football match, a sniper fired upon the stadium. There was a part of the field that was reserved for athletics and that was where he hid himself, and I mean the sniper, and this was one instance when the BH army violated a cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were mentioning the offensive. Were you in your trenches at the time or were you perhaps deployed to a different position for the duration of the offensive? Did you take part in any combat activities in that context?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't anywhere else. I was in the trenches throughout the war and when the offensive was launched I was in the area of Golo Brdo. I will never forget that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me just ask you this, I'm referring primarily to this period of time although I'm referring to the entire period generally. How many civilian victims were there in the area where you were present?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: As formulated, Your Honour, I'd suggest this calls for pure speculation on the part of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Why? This is an area where he was present. He can say it. I don't agree with you, Ms. Edgerton. You may cross-examine him as to his knowledge, the basis of his knowledge.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How many civilians were there, in the area where you lived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Around 20.000 civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And how many civilian victims were there during these clashes?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: Out of around 2.200 fighters of the Sarajevo Brigade, 800 were killed. I don't know the exact number of civilians and I don't want to speculate about that. I do know, however, that some 50 persons were killed by sniper fire in the area from Gornji Hotonj to the neighbourhood of Vogosca. It was from this positions at Hotonj there were civilian victims and soldiers killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sir, you said in your testimony immediately prior to this that you were aware of mass media reports, that there was an exclusion zone of 20 kilometres that had been declared and that there was no heavy weaponry in that zone at the time. Now, perhaps we could probe that a little further. I'd like it know whether by this you're saying that following the declaration of the 20-kilometre exclusion zone there was no heavy weaponry within the area of responsibility of your brigade. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: I know that the weapons concerned were taken away, were driven away, and I never saw them again.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, if I'm not mistaken the area of responsibility of your brigade included Vogosca, included areas like Mrkovici and Poljine. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: In my testimony, I specified quite accurately where I was. What you're referring to was indeed within the area of the 3rd Brigade, but I wasn't there. I was in the area from Zuc all the way to Hotonj. The places you're asking me about, that wasn't in my area. I was a soldier in the trenches and I wasn't able to know about that since I was in the trenches all the time and I didn't have any contacts with the people over there.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you were in the trenches all the time, sir, but I would suggest you were actually very quick to say that all the heavy weapons were removed from the area of responsibility of your brigade and you never saw them again. How, then, did you know that they were removed?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: I know because I saw the weapons being transported away, and I believe they were transported in the direction of Nisici or somewhere there. At any rate, to the south, toward the way out of Vogosca. Nisici is not within the 20-kilometre range.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But Poljine, sir, is within the 20-kilometre range, sir, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: Poljine is indeed. But I don't know what was to be found at Poljine. I told you that I was not there and I cannot testify about that. I have no information.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I would like to ask a map be brought up, please, that might help the witness. It bears the ter number 02786 and if my colleague Madam Registrar would be able to zoom in on the location of Poljine.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sir, what you are about to see will be a map generated by the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps setting out the 20-kilometre exclusion zone and the placement of heavy weapons at weapons collection points within and around that exclusion zone. And once the map comes on the screen, I'm going to direct your attention to Poljine. And I'm sorry, Your Honour, I did communicate the number ahead of time, but, you know, these things do take some time. Longer than I thought, since we'd already had the map up on the screen previously. I'm going to move on to another area and, please, if I could ask the registry if they could indicate to me when the map is visible. I would appreciate that -- oh. Please let me know and I will move on to another area.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sir, do you know, since you know what happened in Vogosca and in the sports hall and at different locations around that area where the weapons collection points were in Vogosca municipality?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: I don't know where those weapon collection points were located, but the weapons, as far as I know, were not at a single point. They -- it was not -- the weapons were not issued from a single point. They would be obtained in various ways.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So, you wouldn't know, then, sir, that there was a weapons collection point in Poljine which housed a 105-millimetre Howitzer, 124 122-millimetre Howitzers, and anti-aircraft guns of all sorts of ranges. You wouldn't know that, then, is that what you're saying, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the witness noted twice what was happening in the area where he was and that he didn't know what was happening at Poljine because he hadn't been there, and now this point about Poljine is insisted on and as he already indicated, he doesn't know about Poljine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But this is a very classical way of cross-examining, Mr. Tapuskovic, I can assure you. There's nothing wrong with it at all. Answer the question, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't really understand your question. If you're asking me if at Poljine I knew anything about that and so on, then my answer is no, and as for the artillery having been at Poljine earlier on, I know about that, I know that I heard that artillery -- artillery had been positioned at Poljine, and was firing from there until the withdrawal and I know about the artillery being positioned at Poljine. Now, as to if I know anything about how the artillery got to Poljine or what you were saying about the distribution, I don't know whether I understood you properly or not. I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think, with that answer, we can actually leave the question of the map, which doesn't seem to have been able to appear on e-court and I can move on to another map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Do I understand you, Witness, to be saying that do you know about the artillery being located at Poljine?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, all right. Thanks. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, well, but he said that it had been deployed at Poljine before the removal. That's what he said. Before the order came to remove the artillery, the heavy weapons. I don't know whether the transcript reflects that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That is consistent with the question that I asked and the answer that he gave.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, sir, are you aware of what kind of weaponry was located at Poljine?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: I don't have any military education, military training, and on the basis of the detonation that I heard I can't now give evidence saying it was this or it was that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sir, do you know the difference between a mortar and a Howitzer?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Were there mortars located at Poljine?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Were there Howitzers located at Poljine?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: I think that they were until the withdrawal of the heavy weapons. I think they were there -- they were there until the withdrawal.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we -- could I ask for document number 3402 to come up on the screen. And I hope that with the effort of the map earlier on I haven't paralysed the system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: Why don't you use ELMO for your map?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If I had the map with me, as big as it is, Your Honours, and it's almost as tall as me, I would have posted it on the screen. But I think we've sufficiently explored that area with the witness. I may look into it during the break time, however. But I'd like to make the most efficient use of the Court time, as I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sir, on the screen in front of you you see a document dated 21 February 1994. It's a Sarajevo-Romanija Corps command document from Colonel --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I have an opportunity to object that had is a document from the 21st of February, 1994 which is the time when Dragomir Milosevic was not the commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What's the implication of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, what does it have to do with the period relevant for the indictment of General Milosevic. This is something that I get so many objections on, that I raise issues that do not pertain to the period relevant for the indictment, which is from August 1994 until November 1995. This document dates from the February --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Now explain the relevance of this.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. The witness has spoken about weapons that were at Poljine and indicated that to the best of his recollection they were only there up until the total exclusion zone was put into force and my intention was -- or proclaimed, I should say. My intention was to put this document -- may I finish my sentence?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not getting any interpretation. I'm not getting any interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm sorry. Should I repeat?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The witness has repeatedly stated that he is aware of heavy weapons having been positioned at Poljine up until the time the total exclusion zone was put into effect, proclaimed into force, and this document, dated 21 February 1994, is a document which lists technical and materiel equipment not pulled out after the date the total exclusion zone was put into force, and I would like to put this document to the witness, given his previous answers, to see whether this might assist with his recollection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, you may.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. If I may just have a moment to go back to my transcript. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, sir, to begin again, the document you see in front of you is an SRK command document from a Colonel Ljuban Kosovac listing the technical and materiel equipment that was not pulled out for a number of different brigades of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. Now, under the heading 3rd Sarajevo Infantry Brigade and that is the second heading on the document, you see it lists a T55 tank remains at Poljine, a 76-millimetre self-propelled gun remains at Poljine and I'm wondering, Witness, if you can say whether that corresponds with your recollection of the situation at that time.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: I don't know how I could have had access to this kind of information. From the beginning of my evidence, I have been telling you that I was in the trench and I had absolutely nothing to do with any of this, and I don't know anything about this. I know that artillery was active from Poljine during the fighting. That's what I know. And I know that after this declaration that the artillery was withdrawn, that it drove past, and I don't have any knowledge as to what may have remained there and this what you just put to me, it simply means nothing to me. I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. So then, with respect to Poljine what -- I take from what you're saying is that you actually don't know whether or not heavy weapons were pulled out of there at all, do you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: Not -- I don't know whether any remained at Poljine or, indeed at any other sites.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, if you just go a little bit further down the list under the same heading, 3rd Sarajevo Infantry Brigade, you see at item number 6 there is a 76-millimetre self-propelled gun listed at Perivoj. Now Perivoj is the general area of the trench in which you were stationed, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I was at Perivoj.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now does this document which listed a 76-millimetre self- propelled gun at Perivoj by late February 1992 correspond -- 1994 correspond with your recollection?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: I was at Perivoj in February 1994, and this thing that you're asking me about, this cannon, this cannon was not at Perivoj and it couldn't have been at Perivoj because Perivoj, the lines where we were, they were all in the low ground. We were there at -- near Tomica Kuca at Perivoj and BH army forces were positioned on the hills. And this cannon would have had no -- would be of no use. It is a cannon that is used for indirect fire. I don't know whether there are any experts who know what this means but this cannon could not have fired and we prayed to God to get some heavy artillery there because we were in a difficult situation and now you're telling me that this cannon existed there. Is this the gist of your questions, whether this cannon existed or was there?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm asking you whether, based on your recollection of the situation at the time, you having been there, this document corresponds with your recollection.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: No, I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, sir, could we put it this way: Is it the case that your knowledge is so limited to that narrow portion of trench that you fought from that you're not in a position to comment on the document, or are you saying that the document is inaccurate?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: My knowledge was not limited to just this trench. I would have known about this cannon being there in the period that you're talking about had it been there and had it been operating.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, we'll take the break now. You have used so far 21 minutes. Witness, you may leave, because there is another matter that I'd like to deal with. You will leave and then you will return after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In carrying out its work the Chamber has discovered that there are parts of the public transcript that should be redacted in order to protect the identity and whereabouts of a protected witness. May we move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll now take the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Thanks to my registry colleagues for their ingenuity, you see on the screen before you the map we were trying to recreate earlier. So if I may step back I would like to put a couple of questions to the witness in regard to the map.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sir, what you see before you is a map generated by and taken from the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps denoting or setting out the diameter or the radius of the total exclusion zone and the heavy weapons collection points within Sarajevo and their contents. And if could I ask, then, please, Madam Registrar, to zoom in to the points in the area of Poljine. Thank you. Now, just having a look at this map, sir, and what you see there in front of you, are you prepared to agree that when you say heavy weapons were removed, your knowledge is only limited to your specific of the trenches and that in fact a number of heavy weapons were not removed from the city perimeter but remained concentrated around there?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: Either the figures on the amount of weapons or types of weapons or the deployment are not known to me, because I was not a member of artillery. I was in the trench. Now as for how many weapons there were and how many there remained, I only know that some weapons were active before that, and then I observed some weapons being transported out of the area. Whether some of it remained there or not, I don't know. As for the breakdown of weapons in terms of their amounts or type, that sort of information was something I did not have access to.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Even though, sir, and you testified you are from Vogosca, there were weapons collection points at Krivoglavci, Metalka and Zuc? Your assertion is that you are unaware of the collection of heavy weapons at those locations. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: It's not true what you are saying, that I knew about the weapons being collected at Zuc and Metalka. I didn't say that. I don't even know where Metalka is located. I don't know what is called by that name, and I don't know that anything was being collected either there. I know that the artillery pieces were not placed along the lines. They were somewhere behind the lines. I'm not sure where exactly. This is the first time I hear of Metalka, of that location. Perhaps if you explain to me what it was, I could tell you something. As for Zuc --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Let me try one more time. Is your assertion that you were unaware of heavy weapons in weapons collection points within the area of responsibility of your brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of the weapons you're asking me about, what remained after the signing of the agreement and what was transported away.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to tender this map, actually. It goes to the witness's credibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P917, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And if we can revert back to the document that we had, please, on the screen immediately before the break which had the 65 ter number 03402, please. If there's a problem with that, I won't ask any further questions about that document, but simply ask that that document with the ter number 03402 also be tendered as a Prosecution Exhibit which I omitted to do before the break, and I certainly hope that I haven't broken the system of e-court today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we will admit that document, too. Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have any objections to the admission, but I would really like to see the document once more, so I hope the system won't fail us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm assured the document is in the system. It's simply that they're experiencing some difficulties with publishing it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And 65 ter 03402 will become Exhibit P918, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps this will be the only document I'll be interested in for the purposes of my re-examination. That is why I would like the document to be brought up if possible, for the witness to look at it later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Its efforts to ensure publication so that Mr. Tapuskovic will be able to cross-examine -- or to re-examine effectively on it. Now ...

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: To go on to another area which probably gives the e-court system a rest, sir, I'd like to ask you about your meetings with General Milosevic which you said took place during the period of 1994/1995. Now, can we just establish that you only met with him during that period. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: I hadn't known General Milosevic before that period.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you talked about first seeing the General during a visit to the command; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: No. I would see him before that, but I didn't know him before the war. I didn't know who the man was.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's -- do you remember testifying that you saw the General when he came to the command?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: When exactly was that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: I can't recall the date. These are at any rate events that are quite unfortunate and that I should like to forget. But, at any rate, it was 1994 and after he assumed his duty.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So can we say it was between August and December 1994 then?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: Yes, at the battlefield.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What month was it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: Sometime in September, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What command was it? Where did you see him?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: I saw him both at the command of the Blagovac Battalion and at the positions held by the members of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now I'm asking about the specific occasion when you say you saw him in the command and he made a comment about a copy of the Geneva Conventions being placed at a more visible location. When was that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: I would have to find out when it was that Jozo Ivanic was wounded, because the event you're interested in happened several days later. It was in late summer. It must have been again, September of 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And was this at the command of the Blagovac Battalion?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Where was the command of the Blagovac Battalion located?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: It was a private home across from that house. It was Mitar Cvjetic's [phoen] house, who wasn't there during the war. It was some 200 or 300 metres to the right of the factory.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Would you -- what factory, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: The Pretis factory, the TAS factory. It is actually a whole complex of factories there at Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So if Blagovac actually, according to the map, lies to the north of Vogosca, you're saying the Blagovac battalion command is somewhere to the south of the town. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: No. The command was in the village of Blagovac, to the south of Vogosca, or, rather, to the south of Vogosca is where Semizovac is. In Blagovac, in the very village, that's where the command was. The factories are to the east and not to the south of Vogosca. And Blagovac also lies to the east.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perhaps I could ask for a map to be brought up on the screen and if the e-court system still doesn't work, I have a hard copy available with me. It bears the ter number 02617I, and if it makes things go any faster, I'm quite happy to provide my copy. And while we wait for that to come up on the screen, sir, what were you doing at the command if you were a trench soldier, as you testified?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: We would come to the command in order to get papers in -- permitting to us travel and I believe that was the reason why I went to the command, to obtain travel permits.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Who was with the General?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: A driver was with him. I don't know his name.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Who was with you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: There was nobody with me, save for the people who worked there in the command. There was a lady there and a man. The lady was in charge of these personnel affairs, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So if I asked to you give us the names of who else would have heard the General make this commend about the Geneva Conventions, you wouldn't be able to give us any names, would you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: I don't understand. The names of the people working there?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The names of the people who would have heard the General make that same comment that you testified about today.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: Ranko Blagovcanin.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Where is he today?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, what did those Geneva Conventions look like? What colour was the paper?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: This was an excerpt from the Geneva Convention --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't see how the witness would be able to answer what colour the paper was 15 years later.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You know that? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If he can't, then he will say so. Yes, what's your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was typed up and copied, since all the commands were ordered to have these papers. It was either photo copied or duplicated in some other way, and it was an excerpt of -- from the Geneva Convention about the war that was copied on a piece of paper. It was appended in all the commands, including the one in Blagovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, sir, you see a map on the screen in front of you. This is a map generated in August 1995 by the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. Do you see the Blagovac command headquarters on that map? And if I can guide you a little bit you should see Semizovac at the top left-hand corner of the map.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: You're mentioning Semizovac, whereas Semizovac is to the south, Blagovac is not in that direction. Blagovac lies ...

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, would be able to perhaps assist this gentleman in marking the location if he is able to find it?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you see, sir, the Cyrillic writing in the middle of the page with the numbers X-122/6, I think you'll find the village of Blagovac immediately below that writing. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: /6 in very dark black letters at the top of the map on the screen in front of you. Do you see --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: Yes, if this is Blagovac indeed. I'm sorry, I am -- I have impaired vision, so I'm not sure. It says -- yes, X-122, Blagovac, but this isn't the direction of Semizovac, because you see the way the road to Semizovac goes. The main road. The Vogosca-Semizovac road goes in a different direction. It is more to the north than to the west. Yes. If this is Blagovac, the print is so poor, although I do believe, yes, that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Is that where the Blagovac Battalion command was located, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. And in Blagovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Could I ask you with the little electronic tool you have to circle the location where the Blagovac Battalion command was and mark it with a number 1.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's fine. Thank you, sir. Now, that's where you say you saw the accused in this case?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sir, why did you need a travel permit? Because that's why, as I recall you said, you had gone up to the battalion command?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: It's been a long time. But the reasons for my travel were that my family was located in a weekend cottage I had. They would be sometimes located in the weekend cottage, sometimes in Vogosca, and perhaps I had to be -- I had to visit them. That was why I needed a travel permit. At any rate, if I had to travel somewhere, it would have been to my native village where they were located.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, sir, you said you saw the General, the accused in this case, five or six times, including this one time. When was the next time after this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ask him first, of the five or six times, where does this one fall.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Quite so.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sir, did you understand His Honour's question? Of the five or six times you said you saw the General, where does this one instance fall, the beginning, the middle, the end?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: The beginning.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Where, then, did you see him the next time, and when?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: I saw the area of Zuc up at Golo Brdo, in the area of Ugorsko or Jezevi in the barracks down there. It was called the 14, the 17, down there at the 14th or the 17th row, at Hotonj. And I would see him on the right flank, in the middle and on the left flank. So he would be touring the areas very often.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, I saw him in the area of Zuc and up at Golo Brdo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Pardon me, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a question. Sir, the point that you just put down, that's the Blagovac Battalion command, right? Where were your trenches exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My trenches extended from Perivoj on the right flank, across Ugorsko, the area held by the VRS, around the factories all the way to Hotonj or all the way to the other side of Hotonj where one goes out of Hotonj to Kosevo. So from the right flank of Zuc and Perivoj, all the way along the line through to the end of Hotonj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you had to go to the command of the battalion, you had to go there in order to get your permit, your travel permit. That's the reason why you went there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The travel permit was not required if one was moving in the area of Vogosca, where one was assigned militarily. However, the place where my weekend cottage was was outside of the area I was assigned to. Every time you had to go out of the area of your deployment, you had to apply for a travel permit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And, sir, that's as one would expect from a disciplined army. It had tight control over the movement of its soldiers. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: At the time of the tenure of the accused, yes. Which doesn't mean that this was the case in the early days, but at the time he was there, there was military discipline.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And one more question relating to your -- the times you saw the accused. What I'm taking, sir, from your answers is that other than perhaps this one occasion at the command, you didn't have personal face-to-face meetings where you spoke with the accused or shook hands. It was merely sightings of him touring the lines with the troops. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To be quite honest, I didn't understand the question. That's why I wanted to intervene. Although it might not be important, the fact that I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And, Witness, do you understand the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood that you were asking me whether I associated with the accused, and the answer is no. We were at different levels.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So the sightings of him were in fact that sightings of him touring the lines where his soldiers may have been operational.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: On several occasions, four, five, six times, I think it was five times at the lines, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I ask that this map, please, be tendered as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P919, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Moving on to another area and coming close to the conclusion, I wanted to go back to something that you mentioned to Mr. Tapuskovic earlier, and it was about -- it was during the time of the offensive of 1995 where you, as you've said, were acting on the defensive and you mentioned that you had artillery support at that time. And I wonder if you could say what kind of artillery support you had?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: I don't know how the artillery was brought back. I think that the artillery had gone since we now have a map here towards the Semizovac and then from Semizovac further on to the Nisici plateau, which is outside of the 20-kilometre zone. Because from what I was able to observe, it didn't go in this other direction where we had another exit point. It was going in that direction. Now as to your question how the artillery had been brought back, I don't know, but what I do know is that we had artillery support on this position where we were. In the previous tab you were talking to me about the artillery being at Zuc, that I was able to see it. The artillery is never positioned where the trenches are. It is it always placed in the depth of the territory. Now as to where it was, at what points, some of the locations, the names of the locations are unknown to me, I couldn't tell you where it was, what hamlet. It was confusion. It was difficult to bring it back to Poljine and there must be a military regulation prohibiting the artillery from operating from a certain position. The artillery did operate -- did fire from this area in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your indulgence for just a moment, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So based on what you've said just now, and I appreciate that explanation, you -- I understand you're saying you don't know what kind of artillery support you had. Is that correct, or do you actually now the calibre of the artillery support you had?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: Well, my military training is too meagre for me to be able to tell you. But this is a larger artillery, larger calibre artillery. I don't know what calibre of cannon. I can't tell you. But it was heavy. If we talk about artillery, that's a cannon, mortars. I can't tell you the calibre on the basis of the sound, the detonation. I don't have the knowledge to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I don't have any other questions from you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Re-examination, Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown P118. That's a Prosecution Exhibit, P118. That's 65 ter 3400. No, I don't know, I'm looking for a document. I have it written down as P118 dated the 21st of February. That's 3402. That's the 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's the one we just dealt with; that's 918.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Now I would like to pay some attention to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, could you please look at what it stays here. What does it read in this document? We saw the date and what does it say underneath the date?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: List of TMS per unit that was not pulled out.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, now if we look at item 6, that's Perivoj, is that correct, that's where it's listed? That's what my colleague asked you. So you have item 6, Perivoj, could be please read what it says at the side?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: Well, it says 1 SO 76-millimetre. To the right it says unfavourable weather conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So it says that on the 21st of February, 1994, in this geographic area in those areas, what was the weather like in all the Sarajevo municipalities that existed, what was the weather like?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: I was in Perivoj in February. It was terrible. We were snowed in. It was terribly cold and a lot of snow. But let me go back to what I said earlier, Mr. Tapuskovic. I never saw this cannon at Perivoj. And I don't know whether it is possible that the cannon cannot be positioned in the trenches. I can't see how, why is the Prosecution and the Defence asking me if I saw this cannon there at the trenches. I didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That's not what I asked you. On the 21st of February we had the situation as we had.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: Yes, the situation was terrible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you about this period from the 10th of August until the end of the war when the weather improved to a certain extent. Is it possible that everything that UNPROFOR demanded be complied with?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: I think that it would have been science fiction for the vehicles to get to Perivoj. First of all, because the exit from Perivoj towards Tomica Kuca to Reljevo is a road that does not meet any standards. It is a village path leading up there to Perivoj. So I don't really think that any vehicle could have approached Perivoj at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. You answered me that in February, you told me what the weather was like in February and this document reads as it reads. It was signed by who it was signed by. I'm asking you about the Territorial Defence period from the 10th of August until the end of the war, do you know at all what the situation was like regarding the weapons that should have been withdrawn and couldn't have been withdrawn as it's indicated here in February?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KOSARAC
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The answer came before I had risen to submit that it doesn't arise from my cross-examination. In any case, the witness said he had no knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You didn't hear what she said? Are you hearing?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I didn't get the B/C/S interpretation but I don't think it really matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Nothing turns on it, Mr. Tapuskovic. Witness, that concludes your evidence. We thank you for giving it and you may leave now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Our next witness was under protective measures but he no longer seeks those measures, and I hope that I will be finished with him in even less time than I was allotted, which is half an hour. That's Witness T-57.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And if I may, Your Honours, I'll take my leave now and see you again at the end of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, have a very good pleasant holiday, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may be seated. You may begin, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness T-57, you know that I am here to defend General Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: We talked this morning. We have to be as efficient as possible and we have to complete your examination in the time allotted to us. That's the first warning. Secondly, I explained to you this morning that you should speak slowly, so could we please also bear that in mind. Thank you, Your Honours.
