This brings us to the witness, the last witness in this part of the proceedings. Witness, could you please state your name to the Judges?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: My name is Nedeljko Ucur.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But please keep an eye on the screen in front of you so that you can be -- you can know where to start talking. You were born on the 21st of January, 1953?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In Sipovo in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: Yes. Please go slow and don't answer until you see that the cursor has stopped, no matter how short the question. The elementary and the high school, commercial high school you completed in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you were not supposed to answer before now. In fact, could you please wait?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's remark, the witness also completed administration college in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you lived in Sarajevo from 1963 until the start of the conflict? You can answer now.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You were employed in the PTT System in the centre of Sarajevo when it all started?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You lived in Sedrenik until the 12th of July, 1992, and this apartment that was your property, you never came back to him after the outbreak of the hostilities?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you now tell us what happened on the 11th of March, 1995?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: On the 11th of March, 1995, a thing happened that I would not wish on anyone. It's a tragedy. I lost my only child, my daughter, who was less than 11 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us about the circumstances in which it happened?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: It was the cease-fire. I had some time off. I was not on the lines, and in the afternoon because it was one of the best cease-fires. Several had been signed before, so in the afternoon, at around 4.00 p.m., 1600 hours, we were in front of the building. There were three of us in military uniforms and there were three or four women there. The children were playing outside in front of the building and until maybe 4.30, we wanted to go back into the building and they said could we play for maybe two or three minutes more and then we will go back. We went into the building and we didn't really climb to the first floor at all when we heard a shot, and we heard the screams. We went out. Two girls had been shot in the head. One of them was my daughter. They were showing signs of life. We took them to hospital, first to the health care centre and to the Kasindol hospital but it was too late. They couldn't be saved.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us -- I know how difficult it is for you to talk about this and I don't want to take you back to it. This is not something that we should be discussing at length, but I do have to ask you when you left the positions on that day, was there any decision --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Sachdeva chose this moment to rise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I'm very sorry to interrupt, but I just would like to know the location because there is -- which building, where in Sarajevo it this occur.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The building at Grbavica, Rave Jankovic Street. The house number was 59.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And now could you please answer the question that I asked you: Was there a decision related to conditions for leaving the line, the positions with the weapons?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: Well, there must have been a written decision but we heard it orally. When we went back to visit our families, to take a bath, we were told not to take our weapons with us home. All the weapons had to be left at the line.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please, bear in mind that you should not start answering before my entire question has been entered in the transcript. I wish to ask you the following: Did the child ask you for permission to go out and play?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: Yes. I said yes, because I was there with my colleagues. There was a cease-fire. There was no fire on either sides and cease-fire had been adhered to until the 11th.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: There were three soldiers, right, you were there, three soldiers?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: Yes, three soldiers and four women who were sitting down there as they were playing. There were the three of us in uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't want to draw any inferences. Please tell me, you were a fighter of the SRK?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: After this event from the positions where you were -- please wait for my entire question to be entered the transcript before you answer. Out of the positions where you were, were you able to see children on the other side aged 10?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: It is true --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I still don't know where his positions were. That hasn't been elicited. I understand that this incident happened when he went on leave but I don't know where his positions are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Where was your position, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My position was at Dobrinja IV, which is three to five kilometres away from my home. I don't know the exact distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now that you've answered this, tell me, since you were in Dobrinja, which is the nucleus of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Were you able to see over all these years, that is to say from 1992 to 1995, children or civilians on the other side?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: It is true that I had occasion to see them both before this incident and after. There was some ten children playing at a distance of 150 to 200 metres from the separation line I would see them and I never --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Pause there. Did you ever, having experienced a loss of your child, shoot at a child on the other side?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: Never. Only madmen could do such a thing. The children are never to blame. In any part of the world in any war the children are always innocent .

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And before that incident, did you ever fire upon a child, a civilian, an elderly person?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: Never. I would have occasion to see children playing and it never occurred to me to do that. I know that children are children. They are not to blame for anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Were any of you ever issued with an order either written or oral, to fire upon civilians?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: No. There were no such orders either oral or written.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please tell me this. Following this event, among the people who lived in the same area where you lived, were there any reactions to the event, in any sense?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: I was unable to follow any sort of reactions like that. But later on I heard stories, since the bridge was open, then the civilians would go both ways. I heard that when this happened on that same day, at 1500 hours, I don't know in what capacity, Yasushi Akashi landed in -- on the Sarajevo airport. And in order to show Yasushi Akashi that Serbs were firing upon Sarajevo, they tried to provoke the Serb side into firing. However, they resisted and remained consistent in what they were doing. Not a single bullet was fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, I have to ask you now the following question: Did you experience anything at the outset of the conflict which you think had anything to do with your participation in combat? Let me not suggest anything further.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: Yes. It is true that I experienced this and I also have eye-witnesses. On the 10th of June, 1992, around eight persons, eight of us gathered on the 10th in the evening. We were rounded up and we were taken to the central prison in Sarajevo. It was there that we were beaten up. But pure chance, by happenstance I had connections with the former minister Jerko Doko and I managed to get out of that hell of the central prison nine days later. People were taken out into the corridor at night. In one corner you would just have a candle burning, the lights were out, and with the rifle-butt and military boots they would be kicking them for hours after which they would only throw them back into the cells and there was no helping these persons. They could not stand the pain. There were pensioners among us. There were 12 of us in one room, and out of the 12 of us, four were pensioners. Drago Vukovic, the former manager of the Zoil institute who been retired for many years, he was to be used in exchange for some Muslims, since his wife's relative was the chief of -- or, rather was Blagoje Adzic, the chief in Belgrade. But he couldn't do anything about it since it was a different state. He lost his leg. I don't know if he is alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see anyone lose their life there?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: No, not personally but I saw that there was this one lad who was 24 years old who was taken to the Kosevo Hospital but I don't think there was any way his life could be saved.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did this have anything to do with your decision to take up arms?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: Of course it did. As I was released from prison, it was through the interceding of Caritas that I managed to be released at Ilidza on the 12th of July. Of course I feared for my life, for the lives of my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Were you afraid of going through all that ordeal again?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. I was afraid of going back to the prison. That's why I asked to be allowed to leave the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When the fighting started, did you have any reserves? Because there was the decision that you should be engaged in combat but was there some sort of a -- were there some reservations that said that you were not supposed to fire at will?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: Of course there were such reservations, especially with regard to civilians. The order was that one or two respond to fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll take the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I was told that I have 14 minutes left and I will try to complete within that allotted time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I asked you a moment ago a question which you may not have understood. Did you know who lived in the part of Sarajevo controlled by the BH army?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: In Sarajevo, between 50 to 60.000 Serbs remained.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Did this have any significance in the situations when open fighting broke out?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: Yes. It is true that it had some significance. There were quite a few Serbs and it was known that they were pushed into the front lines to dig trenches and for those reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you -- rather, you were an eye-witness to the unfortunate death of your child. Did you witness any other killing of civilians?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: Yes, at Dobrinja and at Dobrinja IV. And more than 600 Serbs were killed at Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Civilians?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How many times were you yourself able to witness the death of a civilian?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: Three times. I saw civilians get killed on three occasions, as I was passing by. A civilian was either wounded or killed on these occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know roughly how many of your brothers in arms were killed?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: Well, there are stories about 600 persons having been killed at Grbavica. Some of them civilians some of them soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me was it difficult to get food and water supplies?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: Yes, particularly with water supplies and electricity supplies, but water was the problem number one. We had some sort of fountains that we used to obtain water.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me show you some photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] DD00-4247 to start with.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is this consistent with the situation as you experienced it with regard to water?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: Yes, as regards water, yes. There was a lack of water and it had to be obtained outdoors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, counsel cannot commence this way, in my submission. Firstly it has to be established where was this -- what is depicted in this photograph, where was this photograph taken, what location, does the witness know, has he seen this photograph before, but to simply show photographs of -- show this photograph and ask questions off the bat, in my submission, is not right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, that is a lesson for you, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I accept this lesson but I was about to ask about that. I showed him the photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I will finish quite soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I want to ask the witness whether he can recognise where this is.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: Yes, I can. This is at Grbavica between Rave Jankovic Street and I don't know what the other street was called. That is where water was supplied. There was water pump.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this photograph be admitted into evidence as a Defence exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is will be exhibit number D354.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have another photograph, because the witness spoke of sniper fire and of victims as a result of sniper fire. I wish to show him another photograph therefor, which is the only one I still want to show, which is DD00-4251.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you read what the sign-post on the tree says?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: Attention, sniper fire or something like that, I can't really make it out. Attention, sniper fire active on the cross-roads.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How many such blocks were to be found at Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: Quite a few, because on the other side opposite the faculty --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Well, it has now been stated by counsel but the witness never said that this was in Grbavica or at least it was never asked of him first, but it's been done now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What's the next question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, can you explain in detail where this is?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: This is somewhere between the community centre of Vaso Pelagic and Rave Jankovic Street toward Zagrebacka Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be exhibit number D355.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I have several questions left and quite short ones. On the day your child went out into the street, did she ask something of you?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: She asked to go out and play. Since there was a cease-fire, she asked to be allowed to play with some of her girlfriends. Since I was on leave, we all went down there out of the building in order that she may play.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And they did not shoot at you?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: No. The three of us were in uniform. They didn't shoot at us. We entered the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This was your only child. Can you tell me did you have any more children later on?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: No. I have no children now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The last question. Where do you live now? Did you ever go back to Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: No, never. I never went there nor will I. I live in Bijeljina now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Good afternoon, witness. My name is Manoj Sachdeva and I'm a --

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: Afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: -- lawyer and I'm going to ask you a few questions today. Firstly can I ask that during the conflict you were posted at Dobrinja, Dobrinja IV for the full period. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you were --

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: On position, my position was there and I lived at Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you were an infantry soldier or did you have any other rank?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: I was a rank and file soldier, an infantry soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And during the conflict what sort of weapons did you have?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: A semi-automatic rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you served in a company; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And in Dobrinja IV, where exactly were your positions? Were they in a trench, were they in a house?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: The position was in a house. Two sides were separated by just a street. Dobrinja IV opposite the church.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: The church, I take it you mean the orthodox church; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: The orthodox church. The name of the street was Indira Gandhi. That's the street that divided us from the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And so you know that church quite well; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: I do know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: If I could ask for 65 ter -- I'm just going show you a photograph, Mr. Ucur. 65 ter 03291 to be brought up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Sir, you see a photograph on the screen there?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: It is actually a little bit of assistance, but you can see the arrow and you would agree that the arrow is marking --

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: The arrow is marking or pointing towards -- pointing at the orthodox church; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: That's not the orthodox church. And I can't see where it points to the orthodox church.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Sir, you see underneath the arrow you see a -- a slim white figure. Isn't that the church, sir?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: I can't see it. The church was not completed. The building started before the war, but I can't see any of it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes, the church was not in use, was it, during the war?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: No, it was not in use.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Perhaps can I show you another photograph to assist you?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: If we could ask for --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And it's impossible, the church was not next to the canal. I don't know how far from the canal the church is. But it was not that close to the canal. That's for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Sir, on this photograph the church is, I suggest to you, not -- it doesn't appear to be close to the canal but you would agree, if you think about it carefully, that that is the church, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: I can't see it at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Very well. I will show you another photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: If I could ask for 65 ter 03292 to be brought up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And, sir, while that is being brought up, you went to your positions which were near the church pretty much every day during the conflict; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: Well, not every day. I'd go when I had some time off, I would rest for two or three days and then I would go back.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, you see a photograph there, sir?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And, sir, you told the Court that during the conflict it was not in use for the purpose that it was built for. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: I did say it was not in use, but I don't know, perhaps the priests would go there from time to time, but I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: But as a member of the 1st Sarajevo Brigade in Dobrinja, you know or at least you are aware that during the conflict the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps positioned soldiers in that church, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: I don't know about that. They were not stationed in the church. We were stationed in a house on the separation line. And the church is further down from the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Well, maybe the use of the word "stationed" is not correct. But you are aware that, on occasion, Sarajevo-Romanija Corps soldiers would go to the church because the church afforded a commanding view of the enemy territory; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: They were not in the church. I can guarantee you that. Well, as for a commanding view, it would be better -- you had a better commanding view from the top floors of the building than from the church.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Well, you just said that you don't know about it when I asked you first of all. So now you're saying you do know and that they weren't there. What is it that you know and don't know, sir?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: I know in my case that they were not there, because the church is behind the positions and we had our positions in such a way that it was easier to observe from these high-rise buildings than from the church.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So you were in a high-rise building? Is that what you're saying? Or were there soldiers in the high-rise buildings?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: Yes, in the buildings. The high-rise buildings, because the separation line was such that there were high-rise buildings to both sides of the separation line. Only the street divided us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And so where you were positioned, which I take it now is not a house, and your fellow soldiers, you did as you said a commanding view or a better view of enemy territory; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: A better view. A better view.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And from that position where you were, you and your fellow soldiers, you had your semi-automatic rifles; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And I take it that at least if you spotted or if you came across an ABiH soldier in uniform, you would take that soldier out or at least you would attempt to take the soldier out; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: We didn't try. We didn't shoot. It was cease-fire. There was no shooting from either side. Just this one street divided us. We were in one building on one side of the street, they were in the building on the opposite side of the street. There was no shooting during the cease-fire, but we could see each other but the orders were that there would be no shooting during the cease-fire. Neither side was to fire a single bullet.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So I take it that you're not suggesting that there was a cease-fire from 1992 through to 1995 throughout that full period. So I'm asking you about the period where there was not a cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So in the periods where there was not a cease-fire if you or your fellow soldiers saw or spotted a ABiH soldier, an enemy soldier, you would attempt or you would take that soldier out; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: I wouldn't have tried to take him out. There were several cease-fires. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: But I was talking.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter is not sure whether she heard the answer correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just repeat the last part of your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was -- I became a member of the Republika Srpska army on the 9th of November, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So I take it -- well, you have already told the Court that were positioned in Dobrinja from the onset of the conflict, that is, 1992. So are you saying now that you were not a member of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps up until November 1994; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: Not from the beginning. Not from the beginning. Not from the beginning of the conflict but from the 9th of November, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: What were you doing before that, sir?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: I was undergoing treatment. After I left the federal Sarajevo, I underwent treatment, medical treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So from the period of June or -- well, when you left Sedrenik in July 1992 through to November 1994, your evidence is that you were never stationed at Dobrinja with a semi-automatic rifle with the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So your earlier answers to counsel were not right or at least they were mistaken; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: Well, in what sense were they mistaken? I was talking about the period from which I was a part of a unit of Republika Srpska army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Very well then. From the 9th of November, 1994, through to the end of the conflict, November 1995, December 1995, in the periods where there was not a cease-fire, did you or did your fellow colleagues attempt or take out an ABiH soldier with your weapons if you saw them?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: Well, only if there would be an attack or combat. On other occasions we didn't try anything of the sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So if you saw a soldier with a uniform with a weapon and there was no combat activity and you happened to come across a soldier with the commanding view that you had from your positions, you would not shoot at that soldier. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: I wouldn't, I wouldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: How many times did you use your weapon, sir, in the period November 1994 through to December 1995? How many times did you shoot into enemy area?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how many times. I couldn't really tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Is --

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: Very few times, but I don't know how many times.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: If it's very few times then surely you should be able to remember, sir.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: Well, I can't really say whether it was five, ten or fifteen times. How could I remember such a thing in light of the tragedy that I had?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Is it perhaps because you shot many more times than that that you can't remember? Is that the reason, sir?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: No, that is not the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Did you ever see or did your fellow soldiers or in fact did you ever shoot at civilians?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: It would never occur to me. I never shot at them nor would I have shot at them. If I had wanted to kill children and civilians I could have done that to my heart's content after the death of my child, but it never ever occurred to me. Only a madman could do something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: How about the -- how about before the death of -- the unfortunate death of your child, did you shoot at civilians?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: Never, ever. And I had opportunity. I could see children playing and I never fired at them and it never occurred to me to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Sir, are you a -- at least for one and a half years you were a military person and I take it that you would agree with me that if one enemy was to engage or take out an enemy soldier, that would be an advantage to that person's army. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: Well, it depends on how you see things and I was not in the army for a year and a half. I was released on the 10th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Well, let me put it this way. You agree, and I think it's common knowledge that the ABiH -- the ABiH 1st Corps in Sarajevo had more men than the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. You agree with that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: I don't know their strategy. I don't know what they had at their disposal, because I was just a rank and file soldier. So I really don't know about their strength.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Well, in any event, if you -- if you were to -- or if your fellow soldiers saw an enemy soldier, then you would agree that taking out that soldier, killing that soldier would be advantageous to you and your soldiers and to your army. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't agree. You repeat the same question a second time. It would -- it would not have been a hit. We would not have hit him. You're asking me the same question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to tender this photograph into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. And you have 12 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be Exhibit number P920.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, since you were positioned in Dobrinja IV over a year or actually less than a year now, it seems, and you spoke earlier about the -- the collection of water and water pumps during the war, are you aware that at -- well, firstly are you aware of the school called the Simon Bolivar school in Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: I don't know about the school, and the same situation with water was in 1994 and 1995 and in 1992 and 1993, so the situation was the same throughout the period.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Simon Bolivar school which is in Dobrinja which is your -- which was where you were positioned. Are you aware that at that school there was a water collection point for civilians living within the Sarajevo confrontation lines? Are you aware of that, sir?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: I don't know about that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Did you ever hear --

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: I know about Grbavica. I don't know about Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Sir, I'm asking you about Dobrinja because as you said to the Court earlier, you were positioned in Dobrinja for almost ten months, so are you now saying that you don't know anything about --

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: I don't know about water at Dobrinja. I do know but I don't know about the stationing of water at Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Did you hear that seven civilians students were killed on the 18th of June 1995 by a mortar at this water collection point in Simon Bolivar school in Dobrinja? Did you hear about that?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. The transcript says students. Students, university students, what are we talking about? We were always talking about children, women, and elderly, so where do we now have university students?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't understand your point.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, Mr. President, we're talking about students. I don't know what this claim is based on, because it is contrary to what is in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva, is this based on the evidence that we have heard or an allegation in the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'll -- it was most possibly my mistake to use the word students, but in any case, seven civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So, witness, you never heard about the killing of civilians at this water collection point. That's your evidence?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: I never heard of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: That's because I was in hospital, different hospitals. I would go there just from time to time and I didn't hear about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: When were you in hospital, sir?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: Well, immediately after the tragedy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And I want to, if you don't mind, just to ask you a few questions about that unfortunate incident. And I won't dwell on it too long. But I just want to confirm with you that you said that you were with three soldiers, is that correct, three soldiers with uniform at the time it happened? Is that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: Two soldiers. I was the third one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And are you aware, sir, that the person responsible for this incident was found and prosecuted and punished? Are you aware of that, sir, by the Federation authorities?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: That's not correct. He was detained in custody for 24 hours. Then he was released and given a weapon again. He was not convicted, and I learned from my colleagues that he was killed in 1998 or 1999 lest he should testify to who had issued him the order. I'm not sure whether this is true or not, but this is the rumour that I heard from the -- from the counsel in Sarajevo who was hired to deal with this issue. He first went to the company commander, then was trying to identify the battalion commander and so on, but apparently this will not work. He was told that this guy was killed in 1998 or 1999. That's the -- that's the information that I received from this attorney who filed a complaint, a legal suit, and I think it was a Dzevad Piskic, a waiter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Well, whatever you heard and whatever rumours you heard, you would agree with me that at least there was -- an investigation was initiated. You agree with that, don't you, sir?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: Well, the investigation was initiated but then it stalled. No news -- there have been no news since 1999 when the file -- the suit was filed. He went there with some pictures of the children in 2001. I asked him what was happening. He explained to me that this guy was killed and he asked for the responsible person and then allegedly his company commander had been killed too and then up the chain of command. It was probably --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... All of this is I have to say I don't see the relevance either of what was done in chief or of the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Sir, I understand that -- that that was a difficult incident for you, but you also must be aware or you also know that similar such incidents took place inside the city of Sarajevo, in that children, elderly persons, women were also killed in Sarajevo by Sarajevo-Romanija Corps gun-fire and shells. You know about that, don't you, sir?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: I know that they would be killed. People were killed on both sides, Dobrinja and Grbavica were on fire. There was shooting from both sides. You can't say that there was no fire from the federal Sarajevo into the parts of Sarajevo controlled by the Serbs. There was gun-fire coming from both sides and it is true that there were victims, casualties, civilians on both sides. This is something that is indisputable.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness speak closer to the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, please move closer to the microphone. You have just two minutes, three minutes left, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I'm not disputing that, sir. I'm just putting to you that the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps soldiers would also fire at civilians, children, women, elderly persons inside the city of Sarajevo. That also took place, did it not?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: Well, let me repeat the same answer. Both sides opened fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And, witness, my last question. You spoke about the -- the plane that was carrying Akashi that landed on the 12th of March in 1995. Do you remember that evidence, sir?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: Yasushi Akashi.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes. You remember giving evidence about that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And are you aware, sir, that in fact that plane was shot at by the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps forces at the time it was landing? Is that something you're aware about, sir?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: That is not true and what you said about February is not true either. It happened on the 11th of March on the same day. It was around 1500 hours, and what you say about the Serb forces opening fire, that's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: In fact I did say March 1995 perhaps there was a misinterpretation. Well, I'm going to put it to you, sir, that the commander of the United Nations forces at the time, General Rupert Smith has given evidence here saying that the plane was shot at beyond a reasonable doubt by the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. Do you still maintain your evidence?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO UCUR
utterances.text: I don't know about that. But I really doubt it, because if they had fired then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... What is the objection, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My objection is that we should find that page of the transcript where Rupert Smith stated this in order for the testimony to be put to the witness properly. Because we -- or to do it the way Mr. Sachdeva sought that it be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Don't you remember, Mr. Rupert Smith giving that evidence? I remember that. I don't consider that to be necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I can provide it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is important is for the witness to say whether, having heard that, whether he maintains his position.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I really doubt that the Serb forces would have been shooting, because had they intended to shoot, then they would have responded to the provocations from the other side. However, after the tragedy not a single bullet was fired. I really doubt that they did fire upon the plane.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva, that's the half an hour allotted to you. Any re-examination, Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, since you said that the examination-in-chief wasn't relevant either, then I do not have any questions in re-examination either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Only marginally relevant. I don't know why you insist on bringing these witnesses here who have personal and emotional and distressing evidence to give when it doesn't have any direct bearing on the criminal liability of the accused. Witness, that concludes your evidence. We thank you for coming to the Tribunal and we sympathize with you for the tragedy that you have suffered.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may leave now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, we are at the -- Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not rise to make my closing statement. We will have time for that. But since we filed an application for the certification to appeal the decision of the court of the 26th of July 2007 whereby we were denied the admission of a video-clip, 65 ter number 377D and the transcript, can we just appeal to you to pass down your decision concerning the certification to appeal as soon as possible?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, that will be dealt with, Mr. Tapuskovic, in the -- in the normal way, in the usual way. Mr. Waespi, did you have something to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. We will respond I think in 14 days to this request. We will certainly object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. We are at the end of the session. I'd thank you everyone for working and for the contribution that they have made. And I wish you all a happy and perhaps even prosperous summer holiday. We resume on Tuesday, the 21st of August, at 9.00

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
